content.text:
The latest commit on `origin/main` is one your local copy doesn't have yet. It looks like it was made in the GitHub web editor:

```
b8f4bb5  Remove duplicate headings in README.md   ← last commit (only on GitHub)
aab6464  first commit                             ← your local main is here
f18db02  first commit
e7f9350  first commit
```

It only removes two duplicate `# upshift` lines from `README.md`. If you remove it, the README goes back to having three `# upshift` headings.

You can remove it in one of two ways:

**Option A: Erase it from history (force-push).** The commit disappears from the GitHub commits page.
```bash
git push --force-with-lease=main:b8f4bb5 origin aab6464:main
```
- This moves `origin/main` back to `aab6464`.
- `--force-with-lease` stops the push if anyone has pushed something else since `b8f4bb5`.
- It doesn't touch your local files, so your staged changes (`upshift/`, `tests/`, `pyproject.toml`, etc.) stay as they are.

**Option B: Undo it with a new commit (no history rewrite).** This is safer if anyone has cloned the repo, but the original commit stays in the history.
```bash
git stash            # set your staged work aside first
git pull             # get b8f4bb5 locally
git revert b8f4bb5   # adds a new commit that undoes it
git push
git stash pop        # bring your staged work back
```

Since this is your personal repo and the commit is tiny, Option A gives you what you asked for. Afterwards, check it with `git log --oneline origin/main`: the top line should be `aab6464 first commit`.

The force-push rewrites the public history on GitHub, so I haven't run anything yet. Should I run Option A?

content.text:
The commit made with your mem0 identity is `e7f9350`, and it's the **first** commit in the repo, not the last:

```
b8f4bb5  harsh-madhav (GitHub web)            Remove duplicate headings in README.md
aab6464  harsh-madhav <...gmail.com>          first commit
f18db02  harsh-madhav <...gmail.com>          first commit
e7f9350  harshgupta-mem0 <harsh.gupta@mem0.ai> first commit   ← this one
```

It's the root commit, so every later commit is built on it. Removing it means rewriting all four commits and force-pushing. Every commit hash changes, but the files end up the same.

There are two ways to get the mem0 identity out of the history:

1. **Change its author to your gmail identity (my recommendation).** The commit stays and all the content stays. Only the name and email change. Command:
   ```bash
   git filter-branch --env-filter '
     if [ "$GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL" = "harsh.gupta@mem0.ai" ]; then
       export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME="harsh-madhav" GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL="harsh.madhav.gupta@gmail.com"
       export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME="harsh-madhav" GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL="harsh.madhav.gupta@gmail.com"
     fi' -- origin/main
   ```
2. **Fold it into the next commit (`f18db02`).** The mem0 commit disappears, and its README line becomes part of your gmail commit. You end up with three commits.

Either way, the steps are:
1. Set your staged work aside: `git stash`
2. Pull `b8f4bb5` down: `git pull --ff-only`
3. Rewrite the history (option 1 or 2)
4. Check the authors: `git log --format='%h %an <%ae> %s'` should show no `mem0.ai`
5. Push: `git push --force-with-lease origin main`
6. Bring your work back: `git stash pop`

One thing to know: GitHub may still show the old commit if someone opens its hash directly, until GitHub cleans up unreferenced commits. It won't appear on the commits page.

Which one do you want, 1 or 2? Once you confirm, I'll run it, including the force-push.
